name: Poa
look_here_first: POA: a BOAT-PROW blade tip and a thin membranous LIGULE can help recognize the bluegrass genus, not the species. Our new licensed photos show these structures on P. annua. Distinguish P. annua (usually low introduced annual, bisexual flowers) from P. arachnifera (Texas native state-level rhizomatous perennial with separate male/female plants and cobwebby basal lemma hairs, especially female flowers) using actual rooted shoots, sex and measured reproductive parts. The female lemma hairs are NOT resolved in the current Texas bluegrass landscape photograph.

recognition.where_to_look_first: Compare existing whole-plant images, then inspect the genuinely photographed boat-prow tip and leaf-collar membrane on P. annua. Those do not discriminate it from Texas bluegrass. Rootstock and flower sex are the major species-level evidence.
priority: Identify Poa from actual prow-tipped blade and membranous ligule, ideally on same plant
Photograph entire mature flowering head at consistent scale: low green annual versus taller spring woolly Texas stand (architecture only)
Verify attached rooted base: usually annual non-rhizomatous P. annua versus connected perennial rhizomes of P. arachnifera
Dissect ripened spikelets and establish bisexual P. annua versus separate staminate/pistillate P. arachnifera
Photograph female Texas lemma bases and dense cobwebby hairs at 20–40×, with actual scale, and compare to sparse male hairs where present
recognition.photo_guardrail: Current native photo has only pale whole-panicle gross characters. Never label individual female lemma hairs, plant sex, or underground rhizomes unless actually resolved.

comparison_lesson.title: Poa: boat-shaped blades are only the beginning
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: POA leaf tips = prow; ANNUA = low introduced grass, normally bisexual florets; TEXAS = rhizomes + separate MALE/FEMALE, females webby below lemma.
quick_split: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — INTRODUCED, usually low cool-season annual. Recognize low soft green flowering tufts, often many small open triangular panicles and folded boat-prow leaf tips. The NEW macro really shows the boat tip, and the NEW four-view photo shows a membrane-like LIGULE at the blade/sheath junction. BOTH details are shared by other Poa: for species confirmation, document an intact rooted tuft (usually no persistent connected rhizomes) and a ripe spikelet of normally bisexual florets. The length of a photographed ligule or green head alone is NOT decisive.

TEXAS BLUEGRASS — a native state-level rhizomatous cool-season PERENNIAL, usually flowering in spring with pale to woolly-looking heads on taller culms. Unlike introduced Poa annua, Texas bluegrass is DIOECIOUS: staminate and pistillate plants are separate, and female florets usually have particularly long cobwebby HAIRS arising around basal lemma/callus; male flowers can also bear sparser hairs. The one archived landscape photograph shows prominent pale flowering heads, not a confirmed female floret, pistil, web tuft, rhizome or Hays voucher. A correct determination requires true reproductive macro plus documented rhizome.
guardrails: Both species can have a folded prow-shaped blade tip and membranous ligule. The two new macros are exact-source P. annua photos showing shared genus clues, not proven P. arachnifera anatomy.
Annual bluegrass usually annual, but turf biotypes may persist; duration cannot be asserted without rooted/seasonal evidence.
P. arachnifera is DIOECIOUS: verify a male and a female as different individuals. Male flowers may have sparser basal hairs; never claim the males are entirely bald.
Some rhizomatous introduced P. pratensis plants also have cobwebby basal lemma hairs, but its florets are generally bisexual. Separate by both sex and rooted rhizomes.
Pale woolly-looking Texas heads in the original photo are not direct evidence of a photographed webby female lemma base.
Native to Texas at state scale is not a BONAP Hays County confirmation; original native-zone flags and species count remain untouched.

field_traits: Genus-only photographed boat-prow tip (Jason Hollinger) and true ligule membrane (Stefan.lefnaer).
Existing full tuft photo demonstrates low green flowering heads but not bisexual florets.
comparisons.lookalike_caution: Contrast native P. arachnifera: perennial connected RHIZOMES and separate male/female flowering individuals; a pistillate female's ripe lemma bases produce dense long cobwebby hair tufts, while P. annua flowers generally bisexual and may have keel/marginal hairs but lacks the massive female web character. Do not guess sex or exact lemma hairs from landscape photos; compare P. pratensis and P. trivialis separately where common lawn grasses overlap.

field_traits: Original Texas field photo shows pale woolly-looking flowering heads, but NO separately verified male/female flower and no hair closeup.
Under live ripe specimen check functional floret sex and a female lemma's actual callus hairs.
comparisons.lookalike_caution: Both P. annua and Texas bluegrass have a membranous ligule and boat-shaped blade tips, so neither clue identifies the native species. Compare reproductive SEX on individually collected florets and actual connected underground rhizomes on same-plant clumps. Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) can also be rhizomatous and may have some basal lemma hairs; its flowers are bisexual, so woolliness alone does not prove P. arachnifera.

what_to_teach_crew: BOAT-PROW tips and a TRUE membrane ligule are POA genus cues, not proof which bluegrass species is in hand.
Use both original actual-source field photos to learn low annua panicles versus Texas bluegrass pale spring flowering stands.
The new Jason Hollinger leaf macro shows a true folded prow; new Stefan.lefnaer four-view photo isolates the membrane ligule and original 10-mm reference. Both belong to ANNUA, not Texas.
On a real intact plant, verify roots/rhizomes: Texas connected sod versus typically annual annua tuft. Avoid digging protected planted prairie sites.
At 20–40× examine FEMALE and MALE Texas flowers separately; recognize functional sex, then image dense female basal lemma webs. Do not assume every fuzzy white head is a female.
Compare rhizomatous but usually bisexual Kentucky bluegrass and annual bluegrass look-alikes; keep local native audit and metrics unchanged.

visual_comparison.title: Poa grass ID — photographed Texas bluegrass female cobweb spikelets and true ligule
visual_comparison.subtitle: Regional source-identified pistillate Poa arachnifera panicles, mature vs green webby female spikelets, detached actual long cobweb basal hairs under photographic scale and exact species membranous ligule. Compare annual P. annua separately; actual attached male/rhizome proof remains missing.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: BOTH share the BOAT TIP and true pale MEMBRANOUS LIGULE. Texas bluegrass = RHIZOMATOUS PERENNIAL + DIOECIOUS female spiderweb hairs (now real source photos); introduced P. annua = usually annual, mostly BISEXUAL florets, no comparable dense female spiderweb tuft.

items.caption: Whole plant photo shows low flowering grass, green leaves, and flowering branches. Neither microscopic lemma characters nor ligule is resolvable.
items.why_it_matters: INTRODUCED annual bluegrass: soft low light-green grass in lawns and paths with small open pale green panicles; folded emerging blades with boat-prow tips and a translucent short membranous ligule. Usually annual, though persistent biotypes occur. True flowers are generally bisexual, unlike dioecious Texas bluegrass.

items.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — boat-prow shaped leaf tip
items.image_role: Flickr/Commons macro photographed in Pasadena at 30×, identified by original photographer as annual bluegrass; illustrates the boat-shaped folded grass leaf TIP, shared by other Poa, not a species diagnostic.
items.caption: The green blade narrows to a blunt folded, keel-like 'prow' tip. The lightened very tip is visible; it may be a worn or dry margin, not a separate auricle. The photographer reported magnification 30×, but supplied no calibrated ruler. This proves the shared Poa leaf tip shape, not annual versus Texas bluegrass.
items.why_it_matters: This is an actual photograph of the genus recognition clue that the former whole-plant picture could not resolve. The tip belongs to Poa annua per source label, but its shape alone never distinguishes P. annua from Texas bluegrass.
items.creator: Jason Hollinger
items.photo_status: Source-credited physically viewed licensed 600×530 Commons photo on 2026-10-21. Source identification not independently voucher-confirmed. General Poa-only character, no ruler or unseen hairs.

items.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — actual membranous ligule and blade/sheath collar
items.image_role: Four-view composite macro of one Austrian source-identified annual-bluegrass blade/sheath junction, with original photographer's genuine 10 mm scale, NOT four individuals.
items.caption: Four source-photo views show the same kind of grass blade/sheath collar. The bottom view exposes the whitish membranous flap (ligule) exactly where green blade separates from the upper sheath. The genuine 10-mm photo scale sits at bottom; do not confuse the entire pale sheath with the ligule or infer its precise size without local measurement.
items.why_it_matters: Teaches the actual part crews must photograph: a thin membranous ligule at the junction, not a tuft of hairs or a leaf tip. Texas bluegrass also has a membranous ligule; the difference lies primarily in reproductive sex and perennial rhizomes.
items.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
items.photo_status: Commons 960×1277 composite photographed in Vienna, exact source and CC BY-SA 4.0 visually verified 2026-10-21; only clearly visible pale membrane and collar marked. Four views of anatomy, not four independent specimens.

items.label: Texas bluegrass — original source photo
items.image_role: Actually visually inspected local JPEG; taxon determination from original source
items.caption: Wide field photo shows many pale fuzzy-looking panicles and flowering culms. Individual female cobwebby lemma hairs and sexual organs are NOT visible enough to verify.
items.why_it_matters: Native TEXAS BLUEGRASS is a rhizomatous sod-forming cool-season PERENNIAL, dioecious with male and female plants. Female spikelet florets have conspicuous cobwebby long hairs at basal lemmas that make whole flowering heads look woolly. A distant fuzzy head is only a clue: a verified female floret macro and rooted rhizomes are needed.

items.image_role: True original Texas Poa arachnifera anatomy triptych of attached leaf blade and sheath, with pale membranous ligule at blade/sheath junction and black/white real scale; no auricles. Left view unopened/side, center and right opened sheath with white upright membrane parts.
items.caption: THIS PHOTO IS TEXAS BLUEGRASS, NOT ANNUAL BLUEGRASS. Bob Harms shows three close views of the actual blade/sheath junction. The thin translucent pale membrane protrudes upward from the top of the green sheath, and the original black-white scale is visible along the side. The central white spike is ligule tissue, NOT a grass awn. Length needs independent pixel-calibrated verification.
